cover.headline: A low-cost urea maker about to lose the special pricing on its best plant: fairly valued, not cheap
cover.lead: Chambal is India's largest private-sector urea maker (3.4 mt a year at one site in Gadepan, Rajasthan; ~10% of national output) and sells imported DAP, MOP and NPK, crop-protection products and, from FY27, technical ammonium nitrate (TAN). Urea earned ~80% of segment EBITDA in FY26. Q1FY27 looked strong (EBITDA +12%) mainly because traded fertiliser bought before the West Asia war sold at a 13.7% margin; PAT fell 5% as the IMACID joint venture lost money. The fact that dominates the next three years is policy: Gadepan-III's NIP-2012 pricing ends in December 2026 and the follow-on formula was undecided on 30-Sep. We cut its EBITDA by ₹3,000 a tonne (~₹390 cr a year), so EPS goes ₹48.8 (FY26) → ₹45.5 → ₹43.8 → ₹47.3 (FY27-29E). We value Chambal the way most of the street does, on **P/E: 8.8x Sep-28E EPS of ₹45.6**, which gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** EV/EBITDA (₹561) and DCF (₹589) are higher; bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}, bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Urea is a cost-plus annuity, and Chambal runs it well
arguments.p: The government fixes the farm price of urea and pays the rest as subsidy: gas is passed through, fixed costs are reimbursed and the producer keeps what it saves against energy norms. Chambal's Gadepan-I and II run 4-6% below their norms and Gadepan-III 2-3% below; the plants sell 32-35 lakh t a year. Urea EBITDA was ₹2,190 cr in FY26 (₹6,431/t, ROCE ~25% on segment capital). That is steady, but it cannot grow without new capacity.

arguments.h: The December 2026 reset is the story for FY28
arguments.p: Gadepan-III (1.27 mt) is paid under the 2012 New Investment Policy: ~US$285/t at a base gas price plus ~US$20/t for each US$1/mmBtu rise in gas. That pricing lasts eight years and ends in December 2026. The government had not decided the replacement by 30-Sep; precedent uses net fixed assets and a return on net worth. Elara cuts the plant's EBITDA/t by about a third, IIFL its EBIT/t from ₹7,494 to ₹4,400. Our ₹3,000/t cut costs ~₹7.3 of EPS a year from FY28.

arguments.h: Traded fertilisers, CPC and TAN add revenue, not much margin
arguments.p: Imported DAP/NPK earned 4.0% EBITDA margin in FY26 (−4.0% in FY23); Q1FY27's 13.7% was a one-off inventory gain. CPC and speciality nutrients earn ~23% on ₹1,203 cr of revenue. The ₹1,645 cr TAN plant started trial production in June 2026; we model ₹720 cr of revenue and ₹180 cr of EBITDA in FY28. Together they replace about half of the Gadepan-III loss: FY28E group EBITDA ₹{{F.ebitda.1|num}} cr vs ₹2,694 cr in FY26.

arguments.h: Valuation: cheap on the street's numbers, fair on ours
arguments.p: Brokers' targets run from ₹500 to ₹610, all above the price, on FY28E EPS of ₹42.9-61.8 (median ₹49.5). Our FY28E EPS is ₹43.8. Chambal's one-year-forward P/E has had a median of 10.1x since 2021; fertiliser peers trade ~12% below their own five-year medians, so we use 8.8x. At ₹409 the stock trades at 9.3x our FY28E EPS: it already prices the reset, but not more than that.

catalysts: The government's pricing formula for Gadepan-III after its NIP-2012 period ends (December 2026): every ₹1,000/t of difference from our assumption moves FY28E EPS by ~₹2.4.
Rabi 2026-27 NBS subsidy rates (pending on 30-Sep-2026): they decide whether traded NPK/DAP stays profitable in H2FY27.
Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): first TAN revenue once the plant is declared commissioned, and how fast traded margins normalise.
A Board decision on the fourth urea plant under NIPU-2026 (financial bids expected by mid-October 2026): ₹9,500-10,000 cr at returns management calls "dilutive".
IMACID's return to profit after the sulphur-driven shutdown, and its expansion to 7 lakh t of P2O5 (April-June 2027).

sections.title: A urea plant with a distribution business and a chemicals project attached

blocks.p: Chambal makes urea (and some surplus ammonia) at three plants on one site at Gadepan, near Kota in Rajasthan, and sells it across 14 states in north, central and west India. Through the same network of 4,918 dealers and 93,000+ retailers it sells imported fertilisers (DAP, TSP, MOP, NPK grades and, since Q1FY27, ammonium sulphate), and crop-protection chemicals, speciality nutrients, biologicals and seeds under the "Uttam" brand, all sourced from other manufacturers. It owns a third of IMACID, a Moroccan phosphoric-acid maker (with Tata Chemicals and OCP), and is commissioning a 2.4 lakh t technical ammonium nitrate plant for the mining and explosives market. The K K Birla family groups (Poddar, Bhartia and Nopany) own 61%.

blocks.p: **Urea is a regulated conversion business.** The government fixes the farm price (MRP) and pays the producer the difference between its assessed cost and the MRP as subsidy. Gas, the main input, is bought from a national pool and passed through at a normative consumption per tonne; fixed costs are reimbursed at set rates. Profit comes from (1) using less energy than the norm, (2) producing above "reassessed capacity", which is paid at gas cost plus a fixed element capped by the import price, and (3) for Gadepan-III until December 2026, a price formula that pays more when gas is dear. **Complex fertilisers are trading**: Chambal buys DAP, MOP and NPK abroad, the government pays a subsidy per kg of nutrient (NBS), and the margin depends on buying well relative to the subsidy and the price farmers will pay. **CPC and seeds** are branded distribution with no manufacturing. **TAN** will be Chambal's first unregulated manufactured product.

blocks.callout: **Corporate actions:** One buyback (Feb-2024: ₹700 cr at ₹450 a share, 3.74% of equity); no bonus, split, rights or QIP found in FY20-FY27 filings reviewed. Dividend ₹11 a share for FY26 (interim ₹5 + final ₹6, ₹441 cr). Promoters bought shares in the market (61.3% in Mar/Jun-2026 vs 60.4% in Mar-2025); about 23% of promoter shares were pledged in Jun-2026. The pattern: Chambal sold every non-core business (textiles, shipping, software) to fund and then de-lever Gadepan-III, and returned cash once the debt was gone. The fourth urea plant would reverse that: the balance sheet would carry project debt again.

sections.title: Indian fertilisers: India is short of urea, and the government sets the returns

blocks.p: India used 39.64 mt of urea in FY26, but made only 29.32 mt (30.64 mt in FY25) and imported 10.38 mt (5.65 mt). Urea sales have grown ~3.78% a year over five years, so the gap is widening, which is why the government approved a new investment policy for 8-9 more gas-based plants (NIPU-2026, 15-Jul-2026). In phosphates the dependence is larger: 66% of the 9.4 mt of DAP sold in FY26 was imported. Three features matter for Chambal. **First, urea returns are administered**: the farm price is fixed, gas is pooled and passed through, and a producer earns a regulated return plus whatever it saves against energy norms. **Second, traded P&K margins depend on the subsidy table** (NBS rates per kg of N, P, K and S, revised each season) and on buying ahead of price rises. **Third, the subsidy bill is a fiscal choice**: ₹1.71 lakh cr was budgeted for FY27 against ₹1.86 lakh cr spent in FY26, before the West Asia war lifted input prices (Elara put the likely outgo at ₹2.19-2.83 lakh cr).

sections.title: Urea: full plants, low energy use, and a profit set by formula

pair.title: Urea revenue by quarter

pair.title: Urea PBIT: steady except in turnaround quarters

bullets: **Full plants.** Sales of 33.8, 33.1, 34.4, 32.6, 34.7, 34.1 lakh t (FY21-26). The plants run above 100% of capacity on a two-year turnaround cycle (management wants three). Q1FY27 sales fell to 6.1 lakh t (8.41) because the Gadepan-I turnaround and an extended Gadepan-II shutdown overlapped; Gadepan-III sold 3.3 lakh t of it.

**Low energy use is the edge.** Gadepan-I and II run 4-6% below the government's energy norms and Gadepan-III 2-3% below (Q3FY26 call); the saving is kept. Norms tighten over time, so this needs continuing investment (₹160-180 cr of routine capex a year, e.g. turbines and CO2 compressors).

**Gas is a pass-through.** Realisation rose from ₹36,893/t (FY26) to ₹46,885/t in Q1FY27 as gas rose to US$17.25/mmBtu (provisional). That higher revenue is cost recovery, not profit: Q1 EBITDA per tonne did rise (to ~₹8,500 incl. ammonia, Elara's estimate, from ~₹6,500), but because Gadepan-III was a larger share of a smaller volume, the rupee was weaker and surplus ammonia sold well. High gas mainly raises working capital (the subsidy is paid later).

**Extra profit pools.** Output above reassessed capacity is paid up to the import parity price (~US$900/t in May 2026); surplus ammonia (~23,000 t in Q1FY26) sold at high prices lifted Q4FY26 and Q1FY27. From FY27 that ammonia feeds the TAN plant instead.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the best-run urea complex in the private sector, but a utility: profit per tonne is set by formulas and volumes by plant capacity. We model 32.5 / 34.5 / 34 lakh t and EBITDA of ₹6,520 / ₹5,270 / ₹5,320 per tonne. The FY28 step-down is the Gadepan-III reset (next chapter) plus the loss of surplus-ammonia sales to the TAN plant.

sections.title: December 2026: Gadepan-III loses the pricing that made it Chambal's best plant

blocks.p: Gadepan-III (1.27 mt a year) started production in 2019 under the New Investment Policy of 2012, which pays new plants a normative price for eight years: about US$285 a tonne at a base gas price, plus about US$20 a tonne for every US$1/mmBtu rise in gas (Q1FY26 call), within a floor and ceiling. When gas and import prices are high, as in FY26-27, that formula pays well above cost. The eight years end in December 2026 ("we are to be in this regime from December 1st onwards"). On 30-Sep the government had started the file and asked for data but had not decided the new basis. Management's only guidance: the precedent "considers the net fixed assets and the return on net worth", normally over a 15-year depreciation life, while Gadepan-III is only eight years old; the outcome "could vary... both positively and negatively", and it will set the template for Matix and HURL's three plants.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is the single biggest number in the investment case, and nobody outside the Department of Fertilizers knows it. A cut of ₹3,000/t is in line with the brokers who model it (Elara, IIFL: both ~₹3,000/t); if the government simply moved Gadepan-III onto Gadepan-I/II-type economics the cut would be larger (~₹4,500/t, our bear case); if it recognised the plant's undepreciated cost with a generous return it could be close to nil. Even with no cut at all the stock would be worth ~₹470 on our multiple: the reset caps the upside, it does not make the stock expensive.

bullets: **Volume came from NPK.** Sales rose from 5.64 lakh t (FY25) to 12.31 lakh t (FY26): DAP/TSP 1.86 → 5.13, NPK 2.13 → 5.83, MOP 1.65 → 1.35. Chambal imported 6.03 lakh t of NPK and 5.01 lakh t of DAP in FY26, largely Russian product. Revenue ₹7,025 cr (+174%).

**Margin history: -4% (FY23), 3.6% (FY24), 6.8% (FY25), 4% (FY26).** DAP is effectively fixed-margin (management cites ~₹1,026/t, about 4% of the MRP); NPK prices are free but capped by what farmers pay relative to DAP. In FY23, when prices spiked, the segment lost ₹419 cr.

**Q1FY27 is not a run-rate.** PBIT rose 67% to ₹239 cr (13.7% margin) because Chambal bought 8.5-9 lakh t from January, before the war lifted prices. Management: margins "will decline as the averaging of the prices happens". Rabi NBS rates were still pending on 30-Sep.

**Why do it at all?** It keeps dealers and farmers buying the full basket from Chambal ("protect dealer relationship and wallet share", AR FY26), and it uses a balance sheet that would otherwise sit in liquid funds. It is not a moat.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we model revenue -2.92% / +6.3% / +7.31% (FY27-29E) at EBITDA margins of 6% / 4% / 4%: FY27 keeps Q1's windfall but gives most of it back in H2; FY28-29 return to FY26's 4%. Every 1 point of margin on ~₹7,250 cr of FY28E revenue is ~₹1.4 of EPS.

bullets: **Growth from new products.** Revenue ₹309 → 472 → 717 → 760 → 926 → 1,203 cr (FY21-26). 17 launches in FY26, 14 planned for FY27 (7 done in Q1); biologicals +57% in FY26, Uttam Pranaam (biogenic nano-phosphorus) volumes up ~250% in 9MFY26; seeds (wheat, mustard, maize, bajra) since FY25.

**Asset-light by design.** Chambal owns no CPC plants: products come from partners (Nichino; long-term agreement with Nutrien; talks with Syngenta and Corteva) and white-label developers. The CFCL-TERI Centre of Excellence aims for 10 patented biological products over five years, the first in FY29.

**Margins.** Segment EBITDA margin 19% (FY23), 20.1% (FY24), 23.1% (FY25), 23.6% (FY26); Q1FY27 PBIT margin 25.2% even as revenue fell 6% on deferred farmer purchases. Segment capital employed is under ₹200 cr, so returns are very high but the business is only ~10% of segment EBITDA.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** a well-run distribution business riding Chambal's urea network. We model revenue +15% / +18% / +16% at 23% / 22.5% / 22.5% EBITDA margin, taking segment EBITDA from ₹283 cr to ₹{{F.seg.cpc.adjEbitda.2|num}} cr (FY29E). It grows, but it cannot offset the Gadepan-III reset alone.

sections.title: Technical ammonium nitrate: Chambal's first unregulated product arrives in a short market

blocks.p: The ₹1,645 cr plant at Gadepan (Casale technology, L&T turnkey contract) makes up to 2.4 lakh t a year of technical ammonium nitrate (TAN) and 2.1 lakh t of weak nitric acid (WNA), the intermediate. TAN goes into explosives for coal and metal mining and infrastructure; India uses ~1.2 mt a year, growing 6-7%, and has relied on imports, largely from Russia, which curbed exports in 2026. The plant uses Chambal's own ammonia (its three plants make a 3-5% surplus) and is close to mining hubs (Singrauli, Nagpur, Hyderabad). WNA and AN-solution production started in June 2026; the high-density AN unit was "very soon" to be commissioned on 31-Jul. Until the whole plant is declared commissioned, sales are credited to the project cost, so Q1FY27 shows no TAN revenue.

But it is small: ~₹180 cr of EBITDA in FY28E is under half of what the Gadepan-III reset takes away, and it diverts ammonia that was being sold at high prices. Management is already studying "horizontal and vertical" TAN expansion; nothing is approved.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: lowest-cost operator in a regulated industry, which is a narrow moat

verdicts: G-I and G-II run 4-6% below the government's energy norms and G-III 2-3% below (Q3FY26 call); Chambal keeps the saving. Gas is a pass-through, so efficiency is the main controllable lever.
3.4 mt at Gadepan (~10% of Indian output): shared utilities, ammonia surplus that now feeds the TAN plant, land, water, rail siding and gas approval for a fourth plant.
Distribution in north and central India
4,918 dealers and 93,000+ retailers in 14 states; urea brings farmers in, which sells traded P&K (12.3 lakh t in FY26) and CPC (₹1,203 cr).
Urea MRP and returns are set by policy (NIP-2012, NUP-2015, NIPU-2026's 12-16% ROE band); DAP is a fixed-margin product; NPK prices capped by affordability.
Asset-light trading of imported fertilisers (4% EBITDA margin in FY26) and sourced agrochemicals (~3% market share); no manufacturing or patents yet (TERI pipeline from FY29).
Keeps Chambal competitive; does not set it apart.
Long-term debt repaid (FY25); short-term borrowings only fund subsidy receivables; can fund a ₹9,500-10,000 cr plant and ride out subsidy delays.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Chambal has a **narrow but real advantage**: three efficient plants on one site, energy use below the norms, a balance sheet that can absorb subsidy delays, and the strongest farmer network in its region. That makes it the lowest-risk urea producer and the natural candidate for new capacity. It does **not** have pricing power: the government sets the urea price and the return, and the NIP-2012 windfall on Gadepan-III was a policy gift with an end date. The trading and CPC businesses are distribution, not franchises. Expect high-teens ROE falling to ~14% after the reset, not a compounding story.

sections.title: Revenue follows gas and fertiliser prices; profit has grown, but on a policy ceiling

blocks.p: Chambal's revenue rose from ₹12,206 cr in FY20 to ₹20,794 cr in FY26, but the path was jagged: +73% in FY23 (record fertiliser prices after the Russia-Ukraine war), −35% in FY24 and −7% in FY25 as prices fell, then +25% in FY26 as traded DAP and NPK volumes more than doubled. Most of that is price, not volume: urea sales have stayed at 32.6-34.7 lakh t a year since FY21 because the three Gadepan plants already run above capacity. Profit has grown more steadily: net profit ₹1,226 cr (FY20), ₹1,566 cr (FY22), ₹1,034 cr (FY23), ₹1,953 cr (FY26). FY26 EPS of ₹48.8 is a record. Q1FY27 EPS was ₹13.1 (−5%), as the IMACID joint venture lost money and finance cost rose.

pair.title: Revenue swings with fertiliser prices
Net profit: a record ₹1,953 cr in FY26
EBITDA margin: high when traded volumes are low
Quarterly profit: Q4 is always the weak quarter

blocks.callout: **Our view:** read the margin with care. Group EBITDA margin falls when Chambal sells more imported fertiliser (a 4% margin business) and rises when it sells less, even if profit per tonne of urea is unchanged. The numbers that matter are urea EBITDA per tonne (₹5,556 in FY24, ₹6,228 in FY25, ₹6,431 in FY26), the traded margin and the IMACID share. The first of these is about to change: Gadepan-III loses its NIP-2012 pricing in December 2026.

sections.title: Debt repaid, a buyback, a TAN plant, and now a ₹10,000 cr question

blocks.p: In FY19-22 Chambal generated ₹6,617 cr of operating cash (FY21 alone ₹6,944 cr as the government cleared subsidy arrears) and spent ₹2,278 cr, mostly to finish Gadepan-III. It used the cash to cut borrowings from ₹10,113 cr (FY20) to ₹3,936 cr (FY21). In FY23-26 operating cash was ₹8,098 cr; capex of ₹2,275 cr went largely into the ₹1,645 cr TAN plant, ₹843 cr into a buyback (Feb-2024: 1.56 cr shares at ₹450, including tax and costs) and the rest into repaying all long-term debt by FY25. FY26 operating cash fell to ₹138 cr because subsidy receivables jumped by ~₹1,700 cr. Dividends were ₹10 a share for FY25 and ₹11 for FY26, a payout of ~23-25%.

blocks.callout: **The next decision is much bigger than anything so far.** Under the National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 (approved 15-Jul-2026) Chambal is preparing a fourth urea plant at Gadepan: ~1.3 mt for ₹9,500-10,000 cr, EBITDA of ~₹12,000-13,500 a tonne, commissioning "within 2030". Financial bids were expected by mid-October; the Board and the government had not approved it on 30-Sep. Management calls the returns "dilutive" versus NIP-2012 (an ROE band of 12-16%) and says a buyback is off the table while projects are in view. We do not model it: it would roughly double gross block, absorb the cash we forecast, and earn returns close to, or only slightly above, our 11.9% cost of equity.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books; the judgement sits in the subsidy line

bullets: **Two-thirds of revenue is a government payment.** ₹13,830 cr of FY26 revenue came from the government at notified rates; the auditor (Price Waterhouse) makes its recognition and recoverability a key audit matter. The receivable is the swing item: ₹368 cr of total receivables at Mar-25, ₹2,075 cr at Mar-26 (adjustments of provisional prices paid on a higher gas cost), ₹3,302 cr at Jun-26.

**No exceptional items.** The FY24-26 consolidated accounts carry none. Screener tags ₹34-99 cr a year of gains on liquid funds as "exceptional"; they are ordinary treasury income, and we keep reported EPS in the valuation history (the forward-P/E median is 10.1x on reported EPS and 10.3x excluding those tags).

**IMACID flatters standalone profit, not consolidated.** The parent books IMACID's dividend (₹155 cr in Q1FY27) as other income and pays tax on it; consolidated accounts replace it with the share of IMACID's profit (−₹25 cr in Q1FY27 after a sulphur-driven shutdown). Hence Q1FY27 standalone PAT +10% but consolidated −5%, and a 29% consolidated tax rate. We use consolidated numbers throughout.
**Tax rate fell structurally.** Chambal moved to the 25.17% regime from FY26 after using up its MAT credit; FY25's 32.7% will not recur.

**TAN pre-commissioning sales are capitalised.** Sales of nitric acid and AN solution since June reduce the project cost instead of appearing as revenue until the plant is declared commissioned. Normal practice, but FY27 TAN revenue will start partway through the year.

**Policy can rewrite past profit.** Subsidy rates and gas pass-through are finalised with a lag (escalation/de-escalation); the Gadepan-III reset will change profit per tonne prospectively, and NBS rates are set after costs are incurred.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** A simple group (no minorities of note, no acquisitions, no impairments), a Big-4-network auditor, contingent liabilities of only ₹177 cr, and cash conversion that is lumpy only because of subsidy timing (operating cash ₹6,944 cr in FY21 when arrears were cleared, ₹138 cr in FY26 when receivables rose). The risks are policy risks, not accounting risks.

sections.title: Debt-free in structure, but the government owes it ₹2,462 cr

blocks.p: Chambal repaid its last long-term loans in FY25. What borrowing remains is short-term and funds one thing: money owed by the government. Subsidy receivables were ₹1,954 cr at Mar-2026 (total trade receivables ₹2,075 cr vs ₹368 cr a year earlier) because provisional urea prices paid earlier on a higher gas price were adjusted downwards, and ₹2,462 cr at Jun-2026. Short-term borrowings were ₹963 cr at Mar-2026; management said net cash was "0-0 almost" then and net debt ~₹200 cr at Jun-2026. Screener shows net cash of ₹570 cr at Mar-2026, but that counts the ₹577 cr IMACID stake (equity-accounted) as an investment. Inventory (₹2,280 cr) is mostly imported DAP/NPK bought ahead of the Kharif season.

blocks.callout: **What the model does with cash and working capital:** the engine holds operating working capital at Mar-2026's 11.2% of revenue. That is high by Chambal's recent standard (about 2% at Mar-2025, nil at Mar-2024) because Mar-2026 caught a subsidy adjustment, and lower than the Jun-2026 peak. We keep it: gas is still dear, a high-price year stretches the subsidy budget, and traded fertilisers (paid by the government with a lag) are now a third of revenue. If receivables return to FY24-25 levels, ~₹1,800 cr more cash would appear. Forecast "net treasury" includes the IMACID stake at book; net cash excluding it rises from roughly nil at Mar-2026 to ~₹4,000 cr by Mar-29E.

sections.title: Ownership: three K K Birla family groups, buying more; foreign funds selling

blocks.p: The founding K K Birla family's three branches control Chambal through equal-sized blocks: The Hindustan Times Ltd (Bhartia) 14.28%, Zuari Industries (Poddar, Adventz group) 14.22% and SIL Investments (Nopany) 8.19%, with related trusts and companies taking promoters to 61.34% in Jun-2026. Promoters have been buying (60.40% at Mar-2025). About 23% of promoter shares were pledged in Jun-2026, a level that has been stable at 22-24% for a year. Foreign investors cut their stake from 20.18% (Mar-2025) to 14.92%; no foreign fund held 1%. HDFC Mutual Fund (2.61%) and Nippon India (1.08%) are the largest outside holders.

sections.title: Our forecasts: EPS slips for two years as the Gadepan-III reset bites

blocks.p: We forecast each segment's revenue and EBITDA margin (segment PBIT plus its D&A) and deduct ~₹70 cr of unallocated items. Urea is built from volume, realisation and EBITDA per tonne (see the Urea chapter); TAN starts from a notional ₹1 cr base because the engine needs one. Depreciation rises to ~₹425 cr in FY27E as the TAN plant is capitalised (we use 4.75% of gross block because the engine holds capital work-in-progress flat). Finance cost is ₹40 cr in FY27E (working-capital loans against subsidy receivables), then ₹15 cr. Tax 26% / 25% / 25%; payout 25%. The model's share count (40.05 cr, FY26 profit ÷ EPS) matches the actual 40.07 cr, and minorities are negligible, so EPS needs no adjustment. Every assumption is in the Excel model's Assumptions sheet.

sections.title: The street: all targets above the price, but the honest notes already model the reset

blocks.p: Latest call per broker by 30-Sep-2026: four Buys (IIFL ₹610, JRK ₹587 (May), SKP ₹566, Elara ₹544) and one Hold (Systematix ₹500); no Sell. Three value the stock on P/E (9.5-14x FY28/Jun-28 EPS) and two on EV/EBITDA (5.6-8x FY28E). Every target is above the ₹409 share price. The bull case is that urea is a safe annuity, the TAN plant and CPC add growth, a fourth plant could lift capacity by ~40% by 2030, and the stock is cheap at 9-10x earnings with a dividend. The bear case is the Gadepan-III reset and a cash pile about to be committed to a lower-return plant. The brokers who model the reset (Elara, IIFL, SKP) cut FY28 earnings below FY26 and still say Buy because the multiple is low; we agree it is low, but it has always been low.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good operator, a known earnings dip, and a fair price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's most efficient private urea complex (3.4 mt, energy use below norms, ~25% segment ROCE), a farmer network that sells ₹8,200 cr a year of other fertilisers and agri-inputs, a third of a Moroccan phosphoric-acid maker, a new TAN plant, and a balance sheet with no long-term debt. Profit is set mostly by government formulas, and the most lucrative formula, Gadepan-III's NIP-2012 pricing, ends in December 2026.

**What you are paying:** 9.3x our FY28E EPS and 9.0x Sep-28E, against a one-year-forward median of 10.1x since 2021 and urea-heavy peers at ~8.8x trailing. On the street's own method with our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}). The stock has fallen ~41% from its May-2025 high (₹695 weekly close) to ₹409: the reset is largely priced, the TAN plant and a fourth urea plant are not, and neither is a worse reset.

rows: The main nitrogen fertiliser (46% N), made from natural gas via ammonia; its farm price (MRP) is fixed by the government.
The pricing rules for older urea plants: gas cost passed through at normative energy use, fixed costs reimbursed at set rates.

New Investment Policy 2012 for new urea plants: an import-linked normative price, rising with gas, for eight years from start of production. Gadepan-III is the main beneficiary; its period ends in December 2026.
National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 (approved 15-Jul-2026): support for 8-9 new gas-based plants with a 12-16% return-on-equity band.
The gas use per tonne of urea (in Gcal) the government reimburses; a plant using less keeps the saving.
Reassessed capacity: the official capacity of a urea plant. Output above it is paid at gas cost plus a fixed element, capped by the import price.
Import parity price: what imported urea would cost delivered in India.
Domestic and imported gas for urea plants is pooled to one price; the Empowered Pool Management Committee manages it.
Di-ammonium phosphate (18-46-0), triple super phosphate, muriate of potash and multi-nutrient "complex" grades: the fertilisers Chambal imports and resells.
Nutrient Based Subsidy: a fixed subsidy per kg of N, P, K and S for P&K fertilisers, set each season (Kharif April-September, Rabi October-March).
Technical ammonium nitrate (an explosives raw material), weak nitric acid (its intermediate), high-density ammonium nitrate (the solid prilled form).
Indo Maroc Phosphore S.A., Chambal's one-third phosphoric-acid joint venture in Morocco with OCP and Tata Chemicals; equity-accounted.
Crop protection chemicals (insecticides, fungicides, herbicides) and speciality nutrients (micronutrients, water-soluble fertilisers, biologicals).
Profit of a segment before interest and tax (PBIT); EBITDA adds back the segment's depreciation.
Cash and investments less borrowings; in this report's forecasts it includes the IMACID stake at book value.
Share price ÷ earnings per share; enterprise value (market value − net cash) ÷ EBITDA.
Discounted cash flow valuation; Ke is the cost of equity (here 11.9% = 6.5% risk-free + 0.9 × 6% equity risk premium).
Long-period average rainfall, used by IMD to define a normal monsoon.
